passage: At the school sports club, the coach split everyone into relay teams. Sarika, new this term, stood at the edge fiddling with her hearing aid. Nobody called her name. Mridul noticed she watched people's lips when they talked. He walked over and faced her directly. "Want to be on our team? You can run third." She nodded, surprised. Before the race, he tapped her shoulder instead of shouting when it was her turn to get ready. She ran fast. After, she said quietly, "Thanks for looking at me when you talk." Mridul grinned. "You're quick. Stay with us next week too."

qa.q: What did Sarika fiddle with at the edge?
qa.a: She was fiddling with her hearing aid.

qa.q: What might Sarika's quiet thanks suggest about how she had been feeling?
qa.a: It suggests she had felt left out and was relieved someone made it easier for her to join.

qa.q: Which of Mridul's choices helped Sarika join in?
qa.a: He invited her, faced her when speaking and tapped her shoulder instead of shouting.

qa.q: How might the team see Sarika after the race?
qa.a: They may see her as a fast teammate, not just the new girl.

grounding: It shows a child making room for a new, shy classmate with a hearing aid.

passage: I'm Sahil, and Vidya sits in front of me. When the new boy came to our class on crutches, most of us just stared. At lunch he sat alone near the steps, because our usual spot is on the grass slope. Vidya picked up her tiffin, walked over and sat next to him. The next day she asked our group to move to the steps. A few of us grumbled. She didn't argue; she just went. I don't know if she felt sorry for him or just liked him. By the end of the week, all of us were eating on the steps, and he was telling jokes.

qa.q: Where did the new boy sit alone at lunch?
qa.a: He sat alone near the steps.

qa.q: What does Sahil think might have been on Vidya's mind?
qa.a: Sahil isn't sure if she felt sorry for the boy or simply liked him.

qa.q: What small step made the biggest difference for the new boy?
qa.a: Vidya moving to eat beside him, and then asking the group to move to the steps.

qa.q: How is the new boy affected by the end of the week?
qa.a: He is no longer alone and feels comfortable enough to tell jokes.

grounding: A classmate observes a child making room for a new classmate with different abilities.

passage:
Day one: Lakshmi joined Class 6 from Kerala. She hardly spoke and ate lunch alone, staring at her book. Dilnaz saw her but didn't know what to say.
Day four: At recess, Dilnaz walked over with a skipping rope. "We need one more to hold the rope. Want to?" Lakshmi hesitated, then took the end.
Week three: Lakshmi taught the group a clapping game from her old school. Everyone got the rhythm wrong and laughed. Lakshmi laughed loudest. Dilnaz noticed she'd started saying "we" instead of "you all."

qa.q: What did Dilnaz bring when walking over on day four?
qa.a: Dilnaz brought a skipping rope.

qa.q: What does Lakshmi saying "we" instead of "you all" suggest?
qa.a: It suggests she now feels she belongs to the group.

qa.q: What could Dilnaz have done on day one?
qa.a: Dilnaz could have simply said hello or asked Lakshmi to join them at lunch.

qa.q: How does Lakshmi's clapping game change the group?
qa.a: The group enjoys something new she brings, which makes her a contributor, not just a newcomer. 😊

grounding: It shows a child including a shy new classmate over several weeks.

passage:
Coach's note, Cooking Club. Written by Siddharth.
This week some boys teased Amandeep (11) for joining cooking club, saying it was for girls. He didn't get angry; he said, "Everyone eats, so everyone can cook." When we made rotis, he asked the girls at his table before taking their rolling pin, and when one said, "Wait, I'm using it," he waited. Later, when a boy grabbed a girl's plait as a joke, Amandeep said, "She doesn't like that. Stop." The boy stopped.
Next: I will ask Amandeep to help me plan next week's pairs, mixing boys and girls.

qa.q: What did Amandeep say when boys teased him about cooking?
qa.a: He said, "Everyone eats, so everyone can cook."

qa.q: What does Amandeep waiting for the rolling pin suggest about him?
qa.a: It suggests he respects others' boundaries and doesn't just take what he wants.

qa.q: How does Siddharth plan to build on Amandeep's example?
qa.a: Siddharth plans to ask Amandeep to help plan mixed pairs of boys and girls.

qa.q: How might the girl whose plait was grabbed feel when Amandeep speaks up?
qa.a: She would likely feel relieved and respected that someone stood up for her.

grounding: A coach's note shows a boy practising courtesy and boundaries without stereotyped roles.

passage:
Saturday night
Today in football practice Elizabeth scored twice against our side. Last month I would've said "girls can't kick" like the other boys do. Honestly she's the best on the field. 👏 I told her "nice goal" and she looked surprised, like she expected me to be rude. That made me feel bad about before.
After practice, two boys pulled her cap off and threw it around. She said "give it back" and they laughed. I caught it and gave it to her. I didn't make a big speech. I just thought, she said stop, so stop.
— Kashish

qa.q: How many goals did Elizabeth score today?
qa.a: She scored twice against Kashish's side.

qa.q: Why did Kashish feel bad when Elizabeth looked surprised?
qa.a: He realised she expected him to be rude because of how he and the other boys had acted before.

qa.q: What could Kashish try next time boys mock Elizabeth?
qa.a: He could tell them calmly to stop and, if it keeps happening, tell the coach.

qa.q: How might Elizabeth see Kashish after he returns her cap?
qa.a: She may start to trust him and see him as someone who respects her.

grounding: A diary shows a boy admiring a girl's skill, dropping stereotypes and respecting her boundaries.

passage: In the small-town school yard, Shalini and Arohi turned the headmaster's old cycle upside down to fix its chain. A group of boys gathered. "Girls fixing cycles? Ha!" said one. Arohi ignored him, pushed the chain back onto the gear and spun the pedal. It clicked into place. The boys went quiet. The next day, one of them came over, holding his own bike. "My chain keeps falling off. Can you show me?" Shalini handed him the spanner. "Hold it like this." He listened carefully and thanked them both.

qa.q: Whose old cycle did the girls fix?
qa.a: They fixed the headmaster's old cycle.

qa.q: What does the boy asking for help the next day suggest about his view?
qa.a: It suggests he now admires the girls' skill and has dropped the idea that girls can't fix cycles.

qa.q: What helped change the boys' minds?
qa.a: The girls calmly showed their skill instead of arguing, then taught the boy respectfully.

qa.q: How might Arohi feel when the boys go quiet?
qa.a: She may feel quietly proud that their work spoke for itself.

grounding: It shows respectful interaction across genders, moving beyond stereotyped roles and mockery.

passage:
Monday: Mohit Uncle at the corner shop gave Zeenat change for a hundred-rupee note, though she had paid with fifty. Nobody noticed. She walked home with the extra money hot in her pocket.
Tuesday: She kept thinking about it in class. Mohit Uncle always gave her a free toffee. What if he got in trouble with his wife over the money?
Wednesday: After school she went back. "Uncle, you gave me too much on Monday. I knew, and I kept it two days. Sorry." Mohit Uncle blinked, counted, then smiled. "I was short fifty that night and couldn't think why. Thank you, beta."

qa.q: What note had Zeenat actually paid with?
qa.a: She had paid with a fifty-rupee note.

qa.q: What does the money feeling "hot in her pocket" suggest?
qa.a: It suggests she felt guilty about keeping money that wasn't hers.

qa.q: Which choice made Zeenat's week end well?
qa.a: She went back, returned the extra money and admitted she had kept it for two days, even though no one knew.

qa.q: How is Mohit Uncle affected by Zeenat's honesty?
qa.a: He is relieved to solve the missing money and grateful to her.

grounding: It shows a child owning up to keeping extra change and returning it, though no one would have caught her.

passage: "Rukmini, let me tell you about the day I broke Headmaster's window. I was eleven, practising cricket in the empty school ground after class. The ball went straight through the glass. Nobody was there. Nobody saw. I could have just walked home. I sat under the tree for a long time, heart thumping. Then I went to his house and told him. He was angry for a minute. Then he said, 'You came yourself. That matters more than the glass.' I paid for it from my savings. That window taught me more than any lesson." Reena Nani laughed. "Now, what did you want to tell me?"

qa.q: Where was Reena practising cricket?
qa.a: She was practising in the empty school ground after class.

qa.q: What does Reena sitting under the tree with her heart thumping show?
qa.a: It shows she was scared and struggling between hiding it and telling the truth.

qa.q: What might Rukmini take from Reena's story?
qa.a: That owning up even when no one saw is worth more than escaping blame.

qa.q: How might the headmaster have seen Reena after she came to him?
qa.a: He seemed to respect her honesty more than he cared about the broken glass.

grounding: An elder tells a story about admitting a mistake when no one would have caught her.

passage: The lunch bell was about to ring. Lalit was alone in the classroom, rushing to get his tiffin from the shelf, when his elbow hit Rashmi Ma'am's globe. It fell and cracked right across Africa. The corridor was empty. He could put it back with the crack facing the wall. Voices came closer. His hands were sweaty. When Rashmi Ma'am walked in, he blurted, "Ma'am, I broke your globe. I'm sorry." She looked at the crack, then at him. "Thank you for telling me. We'll tape it together after lunch."

qa.q: Where did the globe crack?
qa.a: It cracked right across Africa.

qa.q: What do Lalit's sweaty hands suggest?
qa.a: They suggest he was nervous and tempted to hide the damage.

qa.q: What could Rashmi Ma'am do to encourage more honesty in class?
qa.a: She could thank students like Lalit publicly for owning up and respond calmly to mistakes.

qa.q: What would change if Lalit had hidden the crack?
qa.a: He might have got away with it, but he would carry the guilt and lose his teacher's trust if found out.

grounding: It shows a child admitting a mistake when he could have hidden it, under time pressure.

passage: I'm Kashish, and I sit next to Shreya. Today two boys kept talking during the test, so Ma'am said the whole class would lose recess. Everyone groaned. Shreya put her hand up. Her voice shook a bit, but she said, "Ma'am, is it fair to punish everyone for what two people did?" The room went silent. Ma'am thought for a moment. "Maybe not. The two talkers will stay in. The rest can go." I wasn't sure if Shreya was scared or just brave. Maybe both.

qa.q: Why did Ma'am say the whole class would lose recess?
qa.a: Because two boys kept talking during the test.

qa.q: What does Shreya's shaking voice suggest?
qa.a: It suggests she felt nervous about speaking up to the teacher.

qa.q: What could students learn from how Shreya raised her concern?
qa.a: They can question a rule politely with a clear reason instead of complaining.

qa.q: How might Ma'am see Shreya's question?
qa.a: She seems to take it seriously and agree the punishment was unfair to the rest.

grounding: A classmate observes a child questioning whether a group punishment is fair.

passage:
Week one: The school's new rule said anyone late to assembly would miss games period. On Monday the bus broke down and Minakshi missed games. "It wasn't my fault!" she told Rafiq, her father, at dinner. "Is it fair?" he asked. "Not for bus kids."
Week two: Minakshi and three others wrote a letter to the principal explaining that late buses weren't their choice. Rafiq helped with spelling but not ideas.
Week three: The principal changed the rule: bus delays wouldn't count. Minakshi ran to games period grinning.

qa.q: What broke down on Monday?
qa.a: The bus broke down.

qa.q: What does Minakshi's "It wasn't my fault!" show about her feelings?
qa.a: It shows she felt the punishment was unfair and frustrating.

qa.q: What went right in how Minakshi challenged the rule?
qa.a: She and others wrote a clear, polite letter explaining why the rule was unfair to bus children.

qa.q: How might other bus children be affected by the rule change?
qa.a: They won't be punished for delays they can't control, which feels fairer.

grounding: It shows a child judging a rule's fairness and working to make it proportionate over weeks.

passage: "Zainab, you think your team's rule is unfair? Let me tell you about my hockey days. Our coach once benched the whole team for a match because one girl came late. We lost badly. Afterwards I asked him, 'Should eleven people pay for one person's mistake?' He was quiet. The next season he made new rules: the late person runs extra laps, not the whole team. Nobody complained. Fairness means the consequence fits the mistake and the person." Aditi Phuphi sipped her tea. "Now, what's happening in your team?"

qa.q: Why did Aditi's coach bench the whole team?
qa.a: Because one girl came late.

qa.q: What might Aditi have been feeling when she asked the coach her question?
qa.a: She likely felt the punishment was unfair and was frustrated by losing.

qa.q: What lesson does Aditi share about fair consequences?
qa.a: That a consequence should fit the mistake and fall on the person who made it.

qa.q: How might the late girl have felt about the whole team being benched?
qa.a: She probably felt guilty that everyone paid for her mistake.

grounding: An elder tells a story of debating whether a team punishment was proportionate and fair.

passage: In the changing room at his Dublin school, Daniel's voice cracked mid-sentence. Yuki burst out laughing. Daniel went red and wanted to disappear. That evening he asked his dad, quietly, "Is something wrong with my voice? And I've got spots now." His dad sat down with him. "Nothing's wrong. Your body's starting to change. Your voice will settle. Showering every day and using deodorant helps with the sweaty part." Daniel nodded, relieved. The next day, when Yuki's own voice squeaked in class, Daniel just smiled and didn't laugh.

qa.q: What happened to Daniel's voice in the changing room?
qa.a: It cracked mid-sentence.

qa.q: What does Daniel going red and wanting to disappear show about how he felt?
qa.a: It shows he felt embarrassed and ashamed of the change in his voice.

qa.q: What helped Daniel feel less ashamed?
qa.a: His dad explained calmly that his body was changing normally and gave simple hygiene tips.

qa.q: How might Yuki feel when Daniel doesn't laugh at Yuki's squeak?
qa.a: Yuki may feel relieved and grateful, and perhaps realise that laughing at Daniel was unkind.

grounding: It shows a boy understanding early puberty and hygiene without shame.

passage: In the Class 7 health lesson, the teacher put up a diagram about periods. Some boys at the back started giggling. Sachin whispered a joke. The teacher paused. "Half the people in this room will have periods. It's as normal as breathing. Nobody should be laughed at for it." Anirban raised his hand. "Why do they happen?" She explained simply. A week later, a pad fell out of a girl's bag in the corridor. Sachin began to snigger. Anirban said, "Leave it, it's normal. We learned it," and kept walking. The girl picked it up without looking embarrassed.

qa.q: What did the teacher put up in the health lesson?
qa.a: She put up a diagram about periods.

qa.q: Why might the boys at the back have giggled?
qa.a: They probably felt awkward and embarrassed about the topic.

qa.q: What did Anirban do that helped the girl in the corridor?
qa.a: He calmly stopped Sachin's snigger by saying it was normal and walked on, so she wasn't made a spectacle.

qa.q: How might the girl feel if Anirban had joined the laughing?
qa.a: She would likely feel humiliated and ashamed about something normal.

grounding: It shows children understanding menstruation and privacy without shame or mockery.

passage: I'm Kiran, Sudha's older sister. Sudha is eleven, and last month she got her first period at school. She came home quiet and went straight to her room. I knocked. She said she thought something was wrong with her and she'd been scared all afternoon. I'm not sure if she was more scared or embarrassed. I told her it happened to me too, and Mummy sat with us and explained it properly. Now Sudha keeps a small pouch in her bag with pads and a spare pair of shorts, and she even told her friend what to do if it happens to her.

qa.q: What does Sudha now keep in her bag?
qa.a: A small pouch with pads and a spare pair of shorts.

qa.q: What did Sudha think when she got her first period?
qa.a: She thought something was wrong with her and was scared.

qa.q: What helped Sudha feel better?
qa.a: Her sister shared her own experience and Mummy explained it properly.

qa.q: How does Kiran see Sudha's feelings?
qa.a: She isn't sure whether Sudha was more scared or embarrassed, but sees she is now confident enough to help a friend.

grounding: An older sister observes a child learning about menstruation and hygiene without shame.

passage: Every evening for two months, Joseph practised his badminton serve against the wall of their Mumbai building. The watchman got used to the tok-tok sound. At the colony tournament he reached the final against Zubin, who was a year older. Joseph's serves were clean, but Zubin was quicker at the net and won by three points. Joseph's throat felt tight. He walked to the net and shook Zubin's hand. "Your smashes are brilliant." Zubin grinned. "Your serve was tough to return. Practise with me on Sundays?"

qa.q: Where did Joseph practise his badminton serve?
qa.a: He practised against the wall of their Mumbai building.

qa.q: What does Joseph's tight throat suggest?
qa.a: It suggests he felt disappointed and close to tears after losing.

qa.q: Which choice by Joseph showed good sportsmanship?
qa.a: He shook Zubin's hand and praised Zubin's smashes despite feeling upset.

qa.q: How does Zubin respond to Joseph's grace?
qa.a: Zubin praises Joseph's serve and invites him to practise together, showing respect.

grounding: It shows a child building skill through practice and losing gracefully.

passage:
"We lost four–one, Tenzin." Dolma dumped her boots at the door.
"I saw. Your team was tired."
"I missed an easy goal. Everyone saw."
"Did you shake hands after?"
"Yes. I said 'good game.' But I wanted to cry."
"That's still good sport. What will you do?"
Dolma sat on the step. "Practise shooting. Every day before school."
"I'll be in goal. Six-thirty?"
She groaned, then smiled. "Fine. Six-thirty."

qa.q: What was the score of the match?
qa.a: They lost four–one.

qa.q: What does Dolma saying "I wanted to cry" reveal?
qa.a: It reveals she felt very disappointed and embarrassed about missing the goal.

qa.q: What plan does Dolma make to improve?
qa.a: She plans to practise shooting every day before school, with Tenzin in goal.

qa.q: How might Tenzin feel supporting Dolma?
qa.a: Tenzin seems caring and willing to help, offering to get up early to play goalkeeper. 🙂

grounding: It shows a child losing gracefully and committing to repeated practice.

passage: I'm Bidisha. When I was twelve, our kabaddi team reached the district final. For weeks I'd practised my raids every evening in the school ground until my knees were scraped. In the final, Kalyani's team was faster. I got tagged out twice and we lost. I wanted to kick the mat. Instead, I lined up with everyone and shook hands. When I reached Kalyani, I said, "You were too good today." She said, "Your raid in the first half scared me." I didn't expect that. It made me want to practise even more for next year.

qa.q: What had Bidisha practised every evening?
qa.a: Bidisha practised raids in the school ground.

qa.q: What does Bidisha wanting to kick the mat show?
qa.a: It shows Bidisha felt angry and frustrated after losing.

qa.q: What helped Bidisha lose gracefully?
qa.a: Bidisha lined up, shook hands and congratulated Kalyani despite feeling frustrated.

qa.q: How might Kalyani see Bidisha's congratulations?
qa.a: She seems to respect Bidisha, answering with praise for Bidisha's raid.

grounding: A first-person account of practising a sport and losing gracefully.

passage:
Week one: Abhinav bought chips and a fizzy drink every day from the canteen. By football practice he felt heavy and slow, and he kept stopping to catch his breath.
Week two: Mehak, his mother, packed him roti rolls with paneer and a banana. He grumbled. "Try it for a week," she said.
Week three: Abhinav noticed he could run the whole practice without stopping. He still had chips on Fridays, but on other days he ate his tiffin first. "Maybe it's the banana," he joked.

qa.q: What did Mehak pack for Abhinav in week two?
qa.a: She packed him roti rolls with paneer and a banana.

qa.q: What does Abhinav grumbling in week two suggest?
qa.a: It suggests he didn't want to give up his usual snacks and was unsure the change would help.

qa.q: What could Abhinav do to keep the new habit going?
qa.a: He could keep eating his tiffin first and save chips for an occasional treat, as he does on Fridays.

qa.q: How might Abhinav's coach see the change?
qa.a: The coach may notice he has more energy and can play the whole practice.

grounding: It shows a child linking food choices to his energy over several weeks.

passage: "Aparna, in my village when I was your age, we ate ragi rotis, dal, vegetables from the field, and buttermilk. Sweets only on festivals. We walked to school and worked in the fields after. I was never tired. When I came to the city, I started eating fried snacks every day. Soon I felt sleepy after lunch and my stomach grumbled all the time. So I went back to simple food most days and kept the snacks for special occasions." Kishore Thatha put a bowl of fruit in front of her. "Your body is growing. Give it good fuel."

qa.q: What did Kishore eat in his village as a child?
qa.a: He ate ragi rotis, dal, vegetables from the field, and buttermilk.

qa.q: What does Kishore feeling sleepy after lunch in the city suggest?
qa.a: It suggests he noticed that fried snacks every day made him feel worse.

qa.q: What advice does Kishore give Aparna?
qa.a: He tells her to eat simple, good food most days because her body is growing, and keep snacks special.

qa.q: How might Aparna see her own snacks after this story?
qa.a: She may start to think about how her food affects her energy and growth.

grounding: An elder tells a story linking food choices to energy, growth and health.

passage: On the school hiking trip, the snack stall at the base of the hill was the last shop before the long climb. Kashish and her brother Lalit had only enough money for one thing each. Lalit grabbed a cold fizzy drink. Kashish hesitated between the drink and a bunch of bananas with a packet of peanuts. She remembered her teacher saying sugary drinks give quick energy that doesn't last. She chose the bananas and peanuts. Halfway up the hill, Lalit was dragging his feet. Kashish shared a banana. "Okay," Lalit panted, "next time I'm copying you."

qa.q: What did Lalit buy at the snack stall?
qa.a: He grabbed a cold fizzy drink.

qa.q: What was Kashish thinking when she hesitated?
qa.a: She was remembering her teacher's point that sugary drinks give quick energy that doesn't last.

qa.q: Which choice worked better for the climb, and why?
qa.a: Bananas and peanuts, because they gave steadier energy while Lalit tired halfway up.

qa.q: How might Lalit see food choices after the hike?
qa.a: He seems to realise Kashish chose better and says he'll copy her next time.

grounding: It shows a child linking food choices to energy on a hike with little money.

passage: I'm Bhupen. At the colony park, a little boy fell off the slide and scraped his knee. He was screaming. Vandana, who's twelve and lives in my building, ran over. She didn't panic. She took him to the tap and rinsed the dirt off with clean water, then pressed a clean hanky on it. Then she said, "Where's your Amma? Let's find her." She carried him to his mother on the bench. I don't know where she learned it, but she looked like she'd done it before.

qa.q: What did Vandana use to press on the cut?
qa.a: She pressed a clean hanky on it.

qa.q: What does Vandana not panicking suggest about her?
qa.a: It suggests she felt confident and knew what to do in that situation.

qa.q: What steps did Vandana follow for the small injury?
qa.a: She rinsed the knee with clean water, pressed a clean hanky on it and took the boy to his mother.

qa.q: How might the little boy's mother see Vandana?
qa.a: She would probably feel grateful and impressed by how calmly Vandana helped.

grounding: An observer describes a child handling a small injury and bringing in an adult.

passage:
Monday: At school, Pooja's class learned the emergency number and practised saying their address clearly. She wrote both on a card and stuck it on the fridge at home.
Thursday: Nazia Aunty next door showed Pooja her first-aid box: bandages, antiseptic, cotton, and the doctor's number taped inside the lid.
The next Sunday: Pooja's grandmother slipped in the bathroom and couldn't get up. Pooja's hands shook, but she called the emergency number from the card, said the address slowly, then ran to fetch Nazia Aunty. Help arrived soon. Later, Nani squeezed her hand.

qa.q: Where did Pooja stick the card with the emergency number?
qa.a: She stuck it on the fridge at home.

qa.q: What do Pooja's shaking hands suggest about how she felt?
qa.a: They suggest she was frightened, even while she did the right things.

qa.q: What preparation helped Pooja act in the emergency?
qa.a: Learning the emergency number, practising her address and putting the card on the fridge.

qa.q: How might Nani feel about Pooja?
qa.a: She probably feels grateful and proud, which is why she squeezed her hand. 🙏

grounding: It shows a child learning emergency contacts and using them when a grandparent falls.

passage: "Raghav, you burned your finger on the tawa? Come, first cool water, from the tap. Keep it there. When I was in scouts, our leader taught us: cool water for burns, clean water for cuts, press on bleeding, and always tell an adult. Once, at camp, a boy fell and cut his hand badly. I pressed a clean cloth on it and sent my friend running for the leader. I was so scared my knees were shaking, but I remembered the steps. And if it's serious, you call the emergency number." Siddharth Mama held Raghav's finger under the tap.

qa.q: What was Siddharth taught to do for burns?
qa.a: He was taught to use cool water for burns.

qa.q: What does Siddharth's shaking knees at camp show?
qa.a: It shows he was frightened but still remembered the steps and acted.

qa.q: What steps does Siddharth teach Raghav?
qa.a: Cool water for burns, clean water for cuts, press on bleeding, tell an adult and call the emergency number if it's serious.

qa.q: How might Raghav feel learning Siddharth Mama was scared too?
qa.a: Raghav may feel less nervous about emergencies, knowing fear is normal and steps still help.

grounding: An elder tells a story teaching basic first aid and when to call for help.

passage: Dilnaz waited until the other children left the counsellor's room. Her voice was small. "Baljeet Ma'am, an older cousin keeps trying to make me sit on his lap and touches me where I don't want. He says it's our secret." She stared at the carpet. "I told my aunt. She said I was imagining it." Baljeet Ma'am put down her pen and moved closer, but not too close. "Thank you for telling me. I believe you. It's not your fault, and it's not a secret you have to keep." She said she would call Dilnaz's mother and the school's safeguarding lead that same day, and she stayed with Dilnaz until they came.

qa.q: What did Dilnaz's aunt say when she first told her?
qa.a: She said Dilnaz was imagining it.

qa.q: Why did Dilnaz stare at the carpet while speaking?
qa.a: She was probably scared and ashamed, and unsure if she would be believed again.

qa.q: What did Baljeet Ma'am do that helped Dilnaz?
qa.a: She said she believed her, that it wasn't her fault and wasn't a secret to keep, then stayed with her and called her mother and the safeguarding lead that same day.

qa.q: What would change if Dilnaz had stopped after her aunt didn't believe her?
qa.a: She might have stayed unsafe and alone, which is why telling again until someone believes you matters. 🤍

grounding: It shows a child reporting unwanted touch and telling again until a trusted adult believes her.

passage:
"Dhruv, can we talk about something important?"
"Is it about homework?"
"No. It's about your body." Sabina sat next to him. "The parts your swimming shorts cover are private. No one should touch them or ask to see them, except a doctor with me there."
"Even family?"
"Even family. And if someone says, 'Keep this secret,' about touching?"
"I tell you."
"Yes. And who else could you tell?"
"Papa. My class teacher."
"And if I don't listen?"
Dhruv thought. "Tell someone else. Keep telling."
"Exactly."

qa.q: What did Sabina say about the parts swimming shorts cover?
qa.a: Sabina said they are private and no one should touch or ask to see them, except a doctor with Sabina there.

qa.q: Why did Dhruv ask "Even family?"

passage: I'm Deepika. Last year, when I was twelve, my friend Tarun stopped wanting to go to his tuition class. He always had an excuse. One evening he told me the tuition teacher had touched him in a way that felt wrong, and said nobody would believe him. My stomach turned over. I remembered what we'd learned in school: private parts are private, and you tell a trusted adult. I said, "I believe you. Let's tell my mother together." We did. My mother listened, then helped his parents go to the school and the police. Tarun doesn't go there anymore. He still says I helped him most by believing him.

qa.q: What did Tarun say the tuition teacher told him?

grounding: A first-person account of a child believing a friend and helping report abuse to trusted adults.

passage:
Week one: Lavanya wanted a book set that cost more than her monthly pocket money. She drew a jar on paper and coloured a bit each time she saved. Her sister Neelam laughed. "You'll give up."
Week two: At the stationery shop, glittery gel pens called to her. She picked them up, then looked at her paper jar and put them back.
Week five: The jar was full. Lavanya bought the book set. That night she told Neelam, "The pens would've been nice. But this is what I really wanted."

passage: "Vishal, when I was twelve, I wanted real football boots. My father said, 'Save for them.' Every week I kept a little of my pocket money in a tin. Then the town fair came, with rides and sweets. My friends spent everything. I spent half my tin on one evening. The next morning I felt terrible. It took me two more months to get back to where I was. When I finally bought those boots, I wore them until they fell apart." Thomas Dadu laughed. "So, what's in your tin, and what's it for?"

qa.q: What did Thomas keep his savings in?
qa.a: He kept them in a tin.

qa.q: What does Thomas feeling terrible the next morning show?
qa.a: It shows he regretted spending on an impulse and losing progress toward his goal.

qa.q: What could Vishal learn from Thomas's story?
qa.a: That impulse spending can set back a real goal, so it helps to decide what you're saving for.

qa.q: How might Thomas's friends have seen his boots later?
qa.a: They may have admired them, knowing he saved for a long time.

grounding: An elder tells a story about saving toward a goal and the cost of an impulse want.

passage: The school fair had begun, and Yusuf had just enough pocket money for one thing. His geometry box had broken that week, and the maths test was on Monday. But the slime stall was glowing green and purple, and his friends were already squishing it. His sister Preeti tugged his sleeve. "What do you need?" Yusuf sighed. "The geometry box." "And what do you want?" "Slime." He stood between the stalls for a long moment. Then he bought the geometry box. Preeti let him hold her slime for five minutes.
